_what: Formulas go between $...$ (LaTeX math, kept as written; everything else is escaped). The first paragraph of every figure and table in the report: what the plot or table is, why it matters in a scientometric study, and its limitation (1-2 sentences). It is the same for every study, so it is written here once and never asked from an AI model. Keys: plot:<picture file without .png> and table:<CSV file>. A table entry may say which columns (cols), how many rows (n) and which column names (rename) the report shows.

plot:document_types.title: Document types
plot:document_types.about: This bar chart counts the documents of each document type. It shows through which channels the field communicates: journal articles carry peer-reviewed findings, conference papers carry early or technical results, and reviews consolidate what is known, so the mix indicates how mature the field is. Its limitation is that the type is the one assigned by the database, which is not always consistent (some reviews are labelled as articles).

plot:document_types_pie.title: Share of the document types
plot:document_types_pie.about: This pie chart shows each document type as a share of all documents, which makes the relative weight of the publication channels easier to see than absolute counts. Its limitation is that small categories (below about one per cent) are hard to read in a pie, so the exact numbers are given in the table.

plot:languages_pie.title: Languages of publication
plot:languages_pie.about: This pie chart shows the languages in which the documents are written. It indicates how international the field is and how much of it is out of reach for readers of one language. Its limitation is that the database mainly indexes journals with an English abstract, so research in other languages is under-represented.

plot:open_access_pie.title: Open access
plot:open_access_pie.about: This pie chart shows how freely the documents can be read: Gold documents are published open in open-access journals, Hybrid Gold open in subscription journals, Bronze free to read without a licence, and Green available as a copy in a repository. Open access matters for the reach of a field and for readers without journal subscriptions. Its limitation is that the status is a snapshot taken at the time of the export and may change.

plot:subject_areas_pie.title: Subject areas
plot:subject_areas_pie.about: This pie chart shows the subject areas of the documents according to the Scopus classification (ASJC). Each document takes the subject areas of its source, so the pie shows shares of all document-subject area assignments, and it measures how interdisciplinary the field is. Its limitations are that the areas describe the journal rather than the document itself, and that documents whose source is not in the Scopus Source List (mostly books) are left out.

plot:subject_areas_bar.title: Documents per subject area
plot:subject_areas_bar.about: This bar chart counts the documents in each subject area, so it shows what share of the documents touches each discipline. Its limitation is that a document can belong to several areas, so the shares add up to more than 100 per cent.

plot:annual_production.title: Annual scientific production
plot:annual_production.about: This chart shows the number of documents per year (bars) together with the citations those documents have received (line). It is the basic indicator of the growth of a field and of the attention its yearly output attracts. Its limitation is that citations accumulate over time, so the citations of recent years are naturally lower and cannot be compared directly with older years.

plot:annual_trend.title: Exponential trend of the annual production
plot:annual_trend.about: A log trend line fits an exponential curve, $N(t) = e^{a + b t}$, to the number of documents per year by a straight-line fit of $\ln N$ against the year. Exponential growth is the classic model of a growing scientific literature (Price's law of growth), and the slope $b$ gives a constant growth rate of $e^{b} - 1$ per year that summarises the whole period in one number. Its limitation is that an exponential cannot saturate, so it describes the observed period but should not be extrapolated far; the year still being indexed is left out of the fit.

plot:average_citations_per_year.title: Average citations per year
plot:average_citations_per_year.about: This chart shows the mean citations per document of each publication year, and the same value divided by the number of years the documents have been citable. The second measure removes most of the effect of age and allows the impact of older and newer cohorts to be compared. Its limitation is that citations take a year or two to start, so even the per-year value is too low for the most recent cohort.

plot:life_cycle.title: Life cycle of the field
plot:life_cycle.about: This chart fits a logistic (S-shaped) curve, $N(t) = K / (1 + e^{-r(t - t_0)})$, to the cumulative number of documents. Such curves describe how a research field emerges, grows fastest at its inflection point $t_0$ and then saturates at a size $K$, so the fit tells in which phase of its life cycle the field is. Its limitation is that $K$ and $t_0$ are uncertain as long as the growth has not visibly slowed down.

plot:top_sources.title: Most productive sources
plot:top_sources.about: This chart ranks the journals, proceedings and books by the number of documents they published on the topic. It shows where the research is concentrated and which outlets a researcher in the field should follow or target. Its limitation is that it measures quantity only; the impact of the sources is examined separately.

plot:bradford.title: Bradford's law
plot:bradford.about: Bradford's law states that when sources are ranked by productivity, a small core of sources carries a third of the literature, and each further third needs a multiple of sources. The plot draws the cumulative number of documents against the logarithm of the source rank and divides the sources into three zones of equal output, which shows how concentrated or scattered the literature is and which sources form its core. Its limitation is that documents without a source title cannot be ranked.

plot:publisher_treemaps.title: Publishers and their sources
plot:publisher_treemaps.about: A treemap divides a rectangle into tiles whose areas are proportional to the values they represent. Here each panel is one of the publishers with the most documents and each tile one of its sources, so the figure shows both how large each publisher is and whether its share rests on one flagship journal or on many. Publisher names were merged first, since the export writes one publisher in many ways. Its limitations are that small tiles can only be labelled with their numbers, that documents without a source title are not drawn, and that the publisher reflects ownership, not the community that edits a journal.

plot:core_countries_pyramid.title: Countries in the core sources
plot:core_countries_pyramid.about: This population pyramid places two counts back to back for each country: its documents in the Bradford core sources (left) and in all other sources (right), with the share in the core. It shows which countries publish in the central venues of the field. Its limitation is that publishing in the core measures the choice of venue, not the quality of the work.

plot:core_countries_heatmap.title: Countries per core source
plot:core_countries_heatmap.about: This heat map shows the number of documents of each leading country in each core source, numbered as in the Bradford plot. It shows which core venues each country prefers. Its limitation is that the counts per cell are small for most countries.

plot:core_countries_cpp.title: Citations of the countries in and outside the core
plot:core_countries_cpp.about: This scatter plot places each country by its citations per document outside the core sources (x) and inside them (y); a country above the diagonal is cited more in the core. It tests whether publishing in the central venues goes with more attention. Only countries with at least three documents on each side are shown. Its limitation is that raw citations still favour older documents.

plot:core_countries_ncs.title: Age-corrected citations of the countries
plot:core_countries_ncs.about: This plot repeats the comparison with the normalised citation score (NCS), which divides a document's citations by the mean of all documents of the same year, so 1 means cited like the average document of its year. It shows whether the advantage of the core holds when the age of the documents is taken into account. Its limitation is the small number of documents for some countries.

plot:core_authors_pyramid.title: Authors in the core sources
plot:core_authors_pyramid.about: This population pyramid shows for each leading author the documents in the Bradford core sources (left) and in other sources (right). It shows which authors publish mainly in the central venues of the field. Its limitation is that authors have few documents, so the shares change strongly with a single document.

plot:core_authors_heatmap.title: Authors per core source
plot:core_authors_heatmap.about: This heat map shows the documents of each leading author in each core source, which reveals the preferred venues of individual researchers. Its limitation is that most cells hold zero or one document.

plot:core_authors_cpp.title: Citations of the authors in and outside the core
plot:core_authors_cpp.about: This scatter plot compares each author's citations per document outside the core (x) and inside it (y). Only authors with at least three documents on each side are shown. Its limitation is that few authors meet this condition, so the comparison rests on a small group.

plot:core_authors_ncs.title: Age-corrected citations of the authors
plot:core_authors_ncs.about: This plot repeats the author comparison with the normalised citation score (1 = cited like the average document of the same year), which removes the effect of document age. Its limitation is again the small number of comparable authors.

plot:core_institutions_pyramid.title: Institutions in the core sources
plot:core_institutions_pyramid.about: This population pyramid shows for each leading institution its documents in the Bradford core sources (left) and in other sources (right), with the share in the core. It shows which institutions publish in the central venues. Its limitation is that institution names are not always written consistently in the database.

plot:core_institutions_heatmap.title: Institutions per core source
plot:core_institutions_heatmap.about: This heat map shows the documents of each leading institution in each core source, which reveals their preferred venues. Its limitation is the small counts per cell.

plot:core_institutions_cpp.title: Citations of the institutions in and outside the core
plot:core_institutions_cpp.about: This scatter plot compares each institution's citations per document outside the core (x) and inside it (y); an institution above the diagonal is cited more in the core. Only institutions with at least three documents on each side are shown. Its limitation is that raw citations favour older documents.

plot:core_institutions_ncs.title: Age-corrected citations of the institutions
plot:core_institutions_ncs.about: This plot repeats the institution comparison with the age-corrected normalised citation score, which shows whether the advantage of the core is real or due to the age of the documents. Its limitation is the small number of documents per institution.

plot:source_h_index.title: Source impact: h-index
plot:source_h_index.about: The h-index of a source is the largest number $h$ such that $h$ of its documents have at least $h$ citations each; it combines productivity and impact in one number. Ranking the sources by their h-index within the data set shows which outlets publish the field's influential work. Its limitation is that the h-index favours sources with many and older documents and ignores how highly the top documents are cited.

plot:source_pyramid_papers_vs_cpp.title: Source impact: documents and citations per document
plot:source_pyramid_papers_vs_cpp.about: This population pyramid places two indicators back to back for each source: its number of documents (left) and its citations per document (right). It shows at a glance whether a source is large, influential or both. Its limitation is that citations per document are unstable for sources with very few documents.

plot:source_pyramid_h_vs_g.title: Source impact: h-index and g-index
plot:source_pyramid_h_vs_g.about: This pyramid compares the h-index (left) with the g-index (right) of each source. The g-index is the largest number $g$ such that the top $g$ documents together have at least $g^2$ citations, so it gives more weight to highly cited documents; comparing the two shows whether a source's impact rests on a few outstanding documents. Its limitation is that the g-index cannot exceed the number of documents of a source.

plot:source_bubble.title: Source impact: productivity against citations
plot:source_bubble.about: This bubble chart places each source by its number of documents (x) and its citations (y); the size of the bubble gives the h-index and its colour the first year of the source in the data set. It shows four dimensions of source performance in one view. Its limitation is that many small sources overlap near the origin, so only the leading ones can be named.

plot:source_dumbbell_h_g.title: Source impact: gap between h-index and g-index
plot:source_dumbbell_h_g.about: This dumbbell chart joins the h-index and the g-index of each source with a line; the length of the line is the gap between them. A long line means that a few highly cited documents carry much of a source's impact, a short one that its citations are spread evenly. Its limitation is that the gap also grows with the number of documents.

plot:source_heatmap.title: Source impact profile
plot:source_heatmap.about: This heat map shows the profile of each leading source on all impact indicators at once (h-, g- and m-index, documents and citations), each scaled from 0 to 1 with the real value written in the cell. It allows sources to be compared on several dimensions without one indicator dominating. Its limitation is that the scaling is relative to the best source, so the colours exaggerate small differences among the weaker sources.

plot:source_cpp_bars.title: Citations per document of the sources
plot:source_cpp_bars.about: Citations per document divide the total citations of a source by its number of documents, which removes the effect of size and measures the average impact of a document in that source. Its limitation is that a single highly cited document can raise the average of a small source strongly.

plot:source_m_vs_year.title: Source impact over time: m-index
plot:source_m_vs_year.about: The m-index divides the h-index by the number of years since a source's first document in the data set, so young and old sources can be compared. The scatter plot places it against the first year, which shows which sources gain impact fastest. Its limitation is that the m-index is unstable for sources that entered only recently.

plot:sources_over_time.title: Growth of the leading sources
plot:sources_over_time.about: This line chart follows the cumulative number of documents of the most productive sources year by year. It shows when each source became important for the field and whether its role is still growing. Its limitation is that it covers only a few sources.

plot:sources_timeline.title: Timeline of the leading sources
plot:sources_timeline.about: This timeline shows a bubble for every year in which a leading source published on the topic; the size gives the number of documents and the colour their citations per year. It combines the timing, the volume and the impact of each source's output. Its limitation is that recent bubbles are pale because their documents have had little time to be cited.

plot:author_bursts.title: Author bursts
plot:author_bursts.about: A burst is a period in which an author publishes clearly more than the overall rate predicts; it is detected with Kleinberg's algorithm, as in the burst history of CiteSpace. The chart shows for each author the strength, the beginning and the end of the strongest burst, with the burst years in red. It identifies authors who were especially active in a certain period. Its limitation is that bursts are weak and uncertain for authors with few documents.

plot:authors_over_time.title: Production of the leading authors over time
plot:authors_over_time.about: This heat map shows the number of documents per year of the most productive authors, which reveals whether their activity is continuous or limited to a few years. Its limitation is that the counts per year are small, so single documents dominate the picture.

plot:authors_timeline.title: Timeline of the leading authors
plot:authors_timeline.about: This timeline places a bubble for every year in which a leading author published, sized by documents and coloured by citations per year. It shows which years of an author's activity were the most influential. Its limitation is that recent years appear weaker because their documents are young.

plot:lotka.title: Author productivity: Lotka's law
plot:lotka.about: Lotka's law states that the number of authors who write n documents falls as $1/n^{\beta}$ with $\beta$ close to 2, so that about 61 per cent of the authors write a single document. The log-log plot compares the observed share of authors with this curve, which shows how productivity is distributed among the authors of a field. Its limitation is that authors are identified by their database author identifier, which sometimes splits or merges people.

plot:author_h_index.title: Author impact
plot:author_h_index.about: This chart ranks the authors by their h-index within the data set, which identifies the researchers whose work on the topic is both productive and well cited. Its limitation is that it counts only the authors' documents in this data set, not their whole careers, so the values are small.

plot:author_radial.title: The leading authors in a radial chart
plot:author_radial.about: This radial bar chart arranges the leading authors around a circle, one bar per author, sorted clockwise by rank; the length of a bar is the author's fractional score and its colour the country the author publishes from. Fractional counting gives every paper a total weight of 1, shared equally by its authors, so it rewards authors who carry a large share of their papers rather than those who appear in large teams. Its limitations are that an author's country is read from the addresses of the papers (a researcher who moved counts for the country named most often), and that a circular layout makes the lengths of distant bars harder to compare than in a straight bar chart.

plot:institution_bursts.title: Institution bursts
plot:institution_bursts.about: This chart shows the periods in which an institution published clearly more than its overall rate predicts (Kleinberg's burst detection), with the burst years in red. It reveals which institutions became suddenly active and when. Its limitation is that a burst at the end of the period may simply mark the beginning of a lasting rise.

plot:top_affiliations.title: Most productive institutions
plot:top_affiliations.about: This chart ranks universities and research centres by their number of documents, which shows where the research capacity of the field lies. Its limitation is that institution names in the database are not always consistent, so parent organisations and their institutes may be counted separately.

plot:affiliations_over_time.title: Growth of the leading institutions
plot:affiliations_over_time.about: This line chart follows the cumulative output of the most productive institutions, which shows when each of them became active in the field. Its limitation is that it covers only the leading institutions.

plot:affiliations_timeline.title: Timeline of the leading institutions
plot:affiliations_timeline.about: This timeline places a bubble for every year in which a leading institution published, sized by documents and coloured by citations per year, which combines activity and impact over time. Its limitation is that recent bubbles are pale because their documents are young.

plot:corresponding_countries.title: Country of the corresponding author
plot:corresponding_countries.about: This stacked bar chart counts the documents by the country of the corresponding author, split into single-country publications (SCP, all authors from one country) and multi-country publications (MCP, at least one foreign co-author). The corresponding author usually leads the work, so the chart shows which countries lead the research and how much they collaborate internationally. Its limitation is that the corresponding author is not always the intellectual leader of a study.

plot:pyramid_scp_vs_mcp.title: National and international publications
plot:pyramid_scp_vs_mcp.about: A population pyramid places two quantities back to back for the same countries, here the single-country publications (SCP) on the left and the multi-country publications (MCP) on the right. It shows at a glance whether a country's research is mainly national or international, which a single total hides. Its limitation is that it shows only the corresponding author's country and not the number of partner countries.

plot:countries_over_time.title: Production of the countries over time
plot:countries_over_time.about: This heat map shows the number of documents per year of the most productive countries, which reveals which countries drive the growth of the field. Its limitation is that the colour scale is dominated by the largest country, so changes in small countries are hard to see.

plot:countries_timeline.title: Timeline of the countries
plot:countries_timeline.about: This timeline places a bubble for every year of each leading country, sized by documents and coloured by citations per year, which combines the growth and the impact of each country's output. Its limitation is the weak colour of recent years, whose documents are young.

plot:radar_countries.title: Country profiles
plot:radar_countries.about: A radar chart draws several indicators on axes around a circle, so that each country forms a shape and their profiles can be compared at once. Here the most productive countries are compared on documents, citations, citations per document, h-index and the share of international documents, each scaled so that the best of the ten most productive countries scores 100. Its limitation is that the area of a shape depends on the order of the axes and should not be compared directly.

plot:country_bursts.title: Country bursts
plot:country_bursts.about: This chart shows the periods in which a country published clearly more than its overall share predicts (Kleinberg's burst detection), with the burst years in red. It reveals when countries became especially active in the field. Its limitation is that a burst is relative to the country's own average, so it does not measure the size of its output.

plot:countries_production.title: Most productive countries
plot:countries_production.about: This bar chart ranks the most productive countries by the number of documents with at least one author from that country, a measure of national research capacity in the field. Its limitation is that counting a document once for each of its countries raises the totals of countries that collaborate much.

plot:most_cited_countries.title: Most cited countries
plot:most_cited_countries.about: This chart shows the total citations of the most productive countries, a measure of the attention their research receives. Its limitation is that total citations favour countries with older output; citations per document partly correct this.

plot:world_map_top15.title: Geographic distribution
plot:world_map_top15.about: The world map marks the most productive countries with their number of documents, which shows the geographic distribution of the research; a document is counted once for each country of its authors. Its limitation is that a map emphasises large countries by their area, so the numbers on the map should be read rather than the colour alone.

plot:top_country_pairs.title: Country collaboration
plot:top_country_pairs.about: This chart ranks the pairs of countries by the number of documents they wrote together, which identifies the strongest international partnerships of the field. Its limitation is that a document with many countries counts for every pair, so large consortia raise several pairs at once.

plot:chord_diagram.title: Collaboration network of the leading countries
plot:chord_diagram.about: A chord diagram arranges the countries on a circle and connects them with bands whose width is the number of joint documents. Here the most productive countries are shown individually and all others are grouped as the rest of the world, so the diagram shows how open each leading country is to collaboration. Its limitation is that grouping the other countries hides with which of them the collaboration takes place.

plot:word_cloud.title: Keywords
plot:word_cloud.about: A word cloud shows the most frequent keywords, with the size of each word following the number of documents that use it. It gives a quick overview of the topics, data sources and methods of a field; spelling variants (plurals and abbreviations in brackets) were merged before counting. Its limitation is that word sizes are hard to compare precisely and the position of a word carries no meaning, so the exact counts are given in the table.

plot:top_cited.title: Most cited documents
plot:top_cited.about: This chart shows the most cited documents, the works that have shaped the field and that its community relies on. Its limitation is that total citations favour older documents; the citations per year in the table partly correct this.

table:02_Main_Information.csv.title: Main information of the data set
table:02_Main_Information.csv.about: The main information table is the standard opening of a scientometric study: it summarises the size, time span, sources, authorship and collaboration of the data set in one place, so that every later figure can be read against these totals. Its limitation is that it describes only what the database indexes.

table:Document_Types.csv.title: Document types in numbers
table:Document_Types.csv.about: This table gives the number and share of the documents of each document type. Its limitation is that the types are those assigned by the database.

table:Languages.csv.title: Languages in numbers
table:Languages.csv.about: This table gives the number and share of the documents in each language. Its limitation is that the database favours journals with an English abstract.

table:Open_Access.csv.title: Open access in numbers
table:Open_Access.csv.about: This table gives the number and share of the documents in each open-access class. Its limitation is that the status is a snapshot of the export date.

table:Subject_Areas.csv.title: Subject areas in numbers
table:Subject_Areas.csv.about: This table lists all subject areas with their documents, their share of the document-area assignments and their share of the matched documents. Its limitation is that subject areas are assigned to sources, not to individual documents, so a document can count in several areas.

table:04_Avg_Citations.csv.title: Production and citations per year
table:04_Avg_Citations.csv.about: This table gives the documents, total citations, mean citations per document, citable years and mean citations per year of every publication year. Its limitation is that the citation counts are a snapshot of the export date.

table:05_Life_Cycle_parameters.csv.title: Parameters of the life-cycle model
table:05_Life_Cycle_parameters.csv.about: This table lists the fitted parameters of the logistic model: $K$ is the estimated final number of documents, $r$ the growth rate, $t_0$ the year of the inflection point and SSE the sum of squared errors of the fit. Its limitation is that $K$ and $t_0$ are uncertain while the growth continues.

table:07_Top_Sources.csv.title: Top sources in numbers
table:07_Top_Sources.csv.about: This table lists the most productive sources with their documents and total citations, which allows a first comparison of productivity and impact. Its limitation is that total citations favour large and old sources.

table:09_Bradford_zones.csv.title: Bradford zones
table:09_Bradford_zones.csv.about: This table gives the number of sources and documents in each Bradford zone, the quantitative basis of the law. Its limitation is that the zone border depends on where the source that crosses one third is placed: the table puts it in the next zone, the plot in the core.

table:Publishers.csv.title: Publishers in numbers
table:Publishers.csv.about: This table ranks the publishers by documents and gives their number of sources, their share of all documents, their citations and citations per document, after the publisher names of the export were merged. Its limitation is that the merging relies on recognising the names, so a rare spelling may stay separate.

table:10_Source_Impact.csv.title: Source impact indicators
table:10_Source_Impact.csv.about: This table lists the impact indicators of the sources with the highest h-index: NP is the number of documents, TC the total citations, PY start the first year of the source in the data set, and h, g and m the h-, g- and m-index. Its limitation is that all indicators are computed within this data set, not over the sources' whole output.

table:14_Author_Over_Time.csv.title: Leading authors per year
table:14_Author_Over_Time.csv.about: This table gives the documents per year of the most productive authors, the data behind the author heat map. Its limitation is that authors with equal totals are ordered arbitrarily.

table:15_Lotka.csv.title: Lotka's law in numbers
table:15_Lotka.csv.about: This table compares the observed number and share of authors with each number of documents with the share expected from Lotka's law with $\beta = 2$. Its limitation is that the high classes contain very few authors.

table:15_Lotka_parameters.csv.title: Parameters of Lotka's law
table:15_Lotka_parameters.csv.about: This table gives the fitted exponent $\beta$, the constant $C$ and the goodness of fit of Lotka's law for this data set. Its limitation is that the fit is dominated by the authors with one or two documents.

table:Author_Summary.csv.title: Author summary
table:Author_Summary.csv.about: This table summarises every author of the data set: the number of publications (NP), the fractional count (NP Frac: each paper counts 1, shared by its authors), the total citations (TC), the first year in the data set and the h-, g- and m-index. It is the basis of the author analyses and shows which researchers contribute most, in volume and in impact. Its limitations are that authors are identified by their Scopus Author ID, which sometimes splits or merges people, and that the indices count only the documents of this data set.

table:16_Author_Impact.csv.title: Leading authors and their impact indicators
table:16_Author_Impact.csv.about: This table lists the leading authors with their h-index (h of their documents have at least h citations each), g-index (their g most cited documents have at least g$^2$ citations together), m-index (the h-index divided by the number of years since their first document), total citations (TC), number of documents (NP) and the year of their first document (PY\_start). Together these show who combines productivity with sustained impact. Its limitation is that the values count only the documents and citations in this data set, so they are lower than the authors' overall indices, and many authors share the same h-index.

table:Author_Bursts.csv.title: Author bursts in numbers
table:Author_Bursts.csv.about: This table lists the first year, the number of documents, and the strength, beginning and end of the strongest burst of the leading authors. Its limitation is that the strength depends on the chosen burst parameters.

table:Author_Radial.csv.title: Leading authors by fractional score
table:Author_Radial.csv.about: This table lists the leading authors with their country, number of publications, fractional score and citations. Its limitation is that the fractional score depends on the number of co-authors, so it favours authors of small teams.

table:17_Top_Affiliations.csv.title: Top institutions in numbers
table:17_Top_Affiliations.csv.about: This table lists the most productive institutions with their documents and total citations, which allows output and impact to be compared. Its limitation is the inconsistency of institution names in the database.

table:Institution_Bursts.csv.title: Institution bursts in numbers
table:Institution_Bursts.csv.about: This table lists the strongest burst of each leading institution with its strength, beginning and end. Its limitation is that the strength depends on the chosen burst parameters.

table:19_Corr_Countries.csv.title: Corresponding countries in numbers
table:19_Corr_Countries.csv.about: This table lists the national (SCP) and international (MCP) documents and the MCP ratio (share of international documents) of the leading countries by corresponding author. Its limitation is that it does not show with which countries the collaboration takes place.

table:20_22_Countries.csv.title: Country production and impact
table:20_22_Countries.csv.about: This table gives the documents, total citations and citations per document of the most productive countries. Its limitation is that total citations favour countries with older output.

table:21_Countries_Over_Time.csv.title: Countries per year
table:21_Countries_Over_Time.csv.about: This table lists the yearly output of the most productive countries, the data behind the country heat map. Its limitation is that a document counts once for each of its countries.

table:Country_Radar.csv.title: Country profiles in numbers
table:Country_Radar.csv.about: This table gives the unscaled indicators behind the radar chart (MCP = share of documents with a co-author from another country). Its limitation is that the h-index favours countries with a large and older output.

table:Country_Bursts.csv.title: Country bursts in numbers
table:Country_Bursts.csv.about: This table lists the strongest burst of each leading country with its strength, beginning and end. Its limitation is that the result depends on the chosen burst parameters.

table:Country_Collaboration.csv.title: Collaborating country pairs
table:Country_Collaboration.csv.about: This table lists the pairs of countries with the most joint documents. Its limitation is that it counts joint documents but does not weight them by the number of partners.

table:Bradford_Core_baseline.csv.title: Core sources against the other sources
table:Bradford_Core_baseline.csv.about: This table compares the documents in the Bradford core sources with those in all other sources, for all documents and for the documents of countries, authors and institutions. Besides citations per document (CPP) it uses the normalised citation score (NCS), which divides a document's citations by the mean of all documents of the same year and so removes the effect of age. Its limitation is that citations measure attention, not quality alone.

table:Bradford_Core.csv.title: Countries in the core sources in numbers
table:Bradford_Core.csv.about: This table lists for the countries with the most documents in the core sources their documents, core documents, core share, and the citations per document (CPP) and normalised citation score (NCS) inside and outside the core. Its limitation is that documents without a source title are left out.

table:Word_Cloud.csv.title: Most used keywords
table:Word_Cloud.csv.about: This table gives the number and share of documents for the most used keywords, the basis of the word cloud. Its limitation is that broad and specific terms are counted side by side, and that documents without keywords are not represented.

table:23_Top_Cited.csv.title: Most cited documents in numbers
table:23_Top_Cited.csv.about: This table lists the most cited documents with their first author, year, source, total citations (TC) and citations per year since publication; the per-year value allows recent and older documents to be compared. Its limitation is that citation counts are a snapshot of the export date.
